title_zh: 第二十二類 煉丹騙

stories.title_en: Refining Elixir in a Deep Pit, with Long Talisman Stakes

paragraphs.en: Since ancient times there has been talk of refining elixirs, of touching iron and turning it into gold. That is an art of immortals, not something the human world possesses. The elixir-refining method handed down in the world uses three taels of fine silver of the best grade, mixed with lead, mercury, cinnabar, and other ingredients, all refined together in a furnace. Each round must be fired for forty-nine days. After the fortieth day, two men must take turns watching the furnace; day and night they may not leave it for a moment. When the elixir is done, you get nine taels. Out of that, subtract the three taels of silver capital, and three more taels go to buying ingredients, so each round yields only three taels of profit. You can refine four times a year, making twelve taels in all, barely enough to feed two men. So even someone who truly possesses this formula would not deign to practice it. The elixir silver it produces can stand up to remelting, but each time it shrinks a little, until it dwindles back to nothing. And this silver cannot serve as mother silver a second time; to refine again, you must take fresh fine silver as the mother. This is the genuine formula as it has been handed down: it costs care and labor and is very hard to carry out. As for wandering alchemists who make elixir refining their pretext for swindling: they use arsenic, realgar, and such substances to cook good silver down to ash and grit, and falsely call it "elixir seed." Then they melt this together with good silver, and it melts back into silver, whereupon they say, "The elixir can transmute into silver." Every one of these is a put-up job, a fraud and a swindle.

There was a Daoist priest who claimed he could refine elixirs. First he took some silver ash and openly smelted a little silver out of it to show people; most were half doubtful, half convinced. One rich man alone believed him and invited him home to refine. The Daoist said, "Refining elixirs is an immortal art. A house is full of foulness and impurity; I fear it cannot succeed there. You should dig a pit in a secluded spot, fourteen feet deep, the bottom just big enough to hold a bed and a furnace, and do the firing there for forty-nine days. A hundred taels of mother silver can be refined into three hundred taels." The rich man did as he said and dug a pit by the back gate, eight feet across and fourteen feet deep. The Daoist went down into the pit, had him spend ten taels of silver buying lead, mercury, cinnabar, and the rest, and first refined the elixir seed, which was finished in three days. The rich man handed over a hundred taels of silver for refining, and each day lowered three meals down to him. The Daoist also told him to find seven solid round logs, each thick as a hand's grip and three and a half feet long, to serve as talismans. He took a thick coir rope, bound it crosswise around the wooden talismans, and every day had them hammered with a great axe. The rich man went to look down at the pit every day. After thirty-some days, the wooden talismans had been driven down little by little until only a foot remained above ground, and he reckoned the silver was nearly ready. The Daoist knew that after a full month the watchers were bound to grow slack. That night he tied one end of the rope around the wrapped silver and ingredients and the other end around his own waist; then he took the seven long talisman stakes, drove them into the pit wall one every two feet, climbed up by hauling on them, pulled the silver up after him, and fled in the dead of night. The next morning, when the meal was sent down, no one below took it. They shone a candle down: the Daoist was gone. They lowered a ladder and went down to look: the silver had all been stolen. Only then did they realize he had climbed out by way of the stakes; plainly, they had been robbed and swindled.

Note: Firing the furnace in a deep pit kept people from suspecting he would flee. But the talisman stakes and the rope were his escape plan, laid well in advance. The very thing that kept people from suspecting was his way out. Let those who come after take warning from this: can elixir refining still be believed?

stories.title_en: Believing in Elixir Refining Brings Ruin on a Whole Family

paragraphs.en: Alchemists use elixir refining to fleece people. Those cheated have been beyond counting through the ages, so clear-eyed people can all see through the fraud and refuse to believe it. There was a certain Daoist named Bing, a master of the art, lame in one leg, who said openly that he had received the true transmission of elixir refining and would not lightly perform it for anyone. His method was to give people elixir seed and let them melt it with copper or lead: it all turned to silver. When he wanted silver himself, he did not need to refine at all; whatever he drew from his hand was silver. If he saw someone in hardship, a twist of his palm would produce silver to give them; or it would come out of his sleeve, and that too was silver. He was generous in giving to the poor, and so people called him the "Half Immortal." Once a host set out silver vessels and a lavish feast to entertain him. When the meal was over, Bing had a rice bucket brought and set on the table, picked up the silver vessels piece by piece, and dropped them into the bucket. When they looked, it was an empty bucket with nothing in it. He said openly, "I have taken them away, and I am not giving them back." If they asked for them politely, he would say, "They are already back in your house, in the place where the vessels were kept." They looked, and there they were. If they demanded them rudely, the vessels were never seen again. This was called having mastered the Five Ghosts' art of transport. Marvels like this, displayed again and again, were enough to stagger and sway people.

There was a rich man named Yao Lu who believed in him. He invited Bing into his home, bowed to him morning and night, honored him with every courtesy, and begged to learn his art. The Daoist accepted the bows without a qualm but would not transmit the art. Every day he sat back and enjoyed the worship, drank himself drunk and slept, woke and wandered about, and took the family's reverence entirely for granted. But he had some power: whoever bowed to him would pour out their heart in devotion, drink with him at the same table, and sing the praises of his Way. Yao Lu's whole household, old and young, maids and menservants, all revered him. Only Lu's wife, Mistress Xin, never believed from first to last, and she urged her husband time and again to cut off this wicked man. Later the Daoist Bing learned of this. He gave two qian of silver to a young servant of the house and said, "When your mistress combs her hair, take one of the hairs that comes out in the comb and bring it to me." The boy brought him one that morning. Once the Daoist had the hair, he worked his spell at once. By mid-morning, Mistress Xin's heart was set on lying with the Daoist. She said to her maid, "My heart feels strange today." By noon it was worse, and she said again, "My heart feels very strange today." By mid-afternoon she could no longer hold herself back and said openly to her waiting-maid, "I used to hate that Daoist Bing bitterly; why do I adore him today? Look at my face. How does it look?" The maid said, "You look as if you want to sleep." After the evening meal, Xin's longing to sleep with the Daoist grew desperate; her only vexation was that the whole family was around. She forced the urge down and privately told the maid, "Tonight you must stay close to me. If I go into the Daoist's room, you must slap me twice across the face, hard. Whatever you do, don't forget." After they had gone to bed and her husband was asleep, Xin threw on an upper garment, left her lower body bare, opened the door, and ran straight for the Daoist's room. The Daoist was just then working his spell, urging on the talisman. The maid hurried after her, crying, "That is the Daoist's room; you must not go!" There was no answer. The Daoist told the maid, "Get outside," and pulled Xin in by the hand. The maid stepped up and slapped her mistress on both cheeks; Xin paid no heed. She struck her face twice more and said, "You have no clothes on." Only then did Xin wake. "I came here in a dream; why is my real body here? Thank heaven you woke me." She took the maid's hand and said, "Quick, come back in with me. How shameful!" In her room she kicked her husband awake and told him the whole story, including how the maid had woken her. Her husband said, "How could such a thing be? You have always hated him; you staged this scene to frame him. If your heart really wanted to go, why would you have told the maid to pull you back? I don't believe this lie." The next day, having no other choice, she told the whole thing to her husband's elder brother. The elder brother ordered his younger brother to drive the Daoist out; Yao Lu would not listen. So the brother went to the county and lodged a charge. The county had the Daoist brought in and given twenty strokes, then put him to the rod, but the beating did not hurt him, so they threw him in jail. The Daoist had plainly entered the jail with nothing on him, yet whatever he drew from his hand was silver. He bribed the jailers with silver and had them buy wine and meat to bring into the jail. The jailers grew still more fawning, hoping to get his formula out of him. Later he was sent up to the prefecture and then to the circuit; at each level the officials had him beaten, but as there was no solid evidence, they would not put him to death. In the end he called in favors, was released, and fled, no one knew where. Yao Lu's whole family, old and young, afterward fell ill and died one after another; they had been poisoned by his sorcery. Only Mistress Xin, chaste and upright, lived on unharmed to a great age. She ran the household, raised the young grandsons to manhood, and died past ninety.

Note: Sorcery strikes from the dark the way a fox-spirit offers its charms: the heart must be crooked first, and only then can it be beguiled. If the heart is upright, walk into a crowd of demons and the demons cannot harm you. So it was that Fu Yi refused to believe a curse could kill him, and the foreign monk died instead; Zhongyan refused to believe a ghost could kill his son, and the ghost never came. Mistress Xin's heart was upright. Though the sorcerer's potent art could cloud her mind, she had the wit to warn her maid beforehand, and in the end she escaped the poison of his wicked lust. So however clever the art, it is no match for an upright human heart. If you meet a sorcerer, hold your heart fast and pay him no mind; what can his evil do then?

stories.title_en: When the Elixir Trick Can't Cheat Him: Poison in the Food

paragraphs.en: In Gutan there was a young man named Ding Yuhong, sharp and quick-witted, who knew all the falseness of the world; no one could deceive him. He chanced to meet an alchemist who claimed he could refine elixirs. Yuhong knew at once that it was a fraud, and decided to use the occasion to swindle the alchemist instead. So he feigned ignorance and plied the man with fussy questions. The alchemist said, "The elixir is an immortal art, handed down since ancient times to good men, meant specially to relieve the poor. First you must gather ingredients and refine them into elixir seed. Then take one qian of silver, melt it together with the seed, and you get three qian; one tael yields three taels." Yuhong asked, "Can you refine more than that?" The alchemist said, "As long as there is elixir seed, even a hundred taels or a thousand can be refined." Yuhong first gave him one qian of silver to refine. The alchemist added three fen of elixir seed, and out came three qian of silver. Yuhong was delighted, gave him a tael to melt, and again got three taels of silver. More delighted still, he invited the alchemist home and waited on him attentively. Whenever the silver was spent, he asked to refine more for spending money, and batch after batch they melted out thirty-odd taels of silver. He simply plied the man with fine words and said he wished to learn the art, but he never put up much silver of his own for the refining, so in the end it was the alchemist's own elixir-seed capital that got swindled away.

The alchemist saw that in the man's house he could do nothing with him, so he said, "My elixir seed is used up. You should bring more silver capital; we will go out to gather ingredients and do a great refining on the road." Yuhong knew perfectly well the man was luring him out to swindle him, but he thought to himself, "If I keep my guard up, how can he swindle me?" What was more, he wanted to cheat the man out of every bit of elixir seed he still carried. So he took fifty taels of silver and set out with him, refusing to produce it for expenses. When the alchemist told him to take out silver to buy things, Yuhong said, "The elixir is for turning into silver. Now that we have finished silver, why spend it lightly? Bring out seed and refine silver for travel expenses; my silver stays for buying ingredients." The alchemist put in all three taels of elixir seed he had left, and Yuhong ten taels of silver; together they refined it into thirty taels, and each took half. They traveled two more days, and Yuhong kept strict guard even over sleep and meals. The alchemist had no scheme by which to get at him, so he secretly bought arsenic and kept it on his person. That evening he also bought a fresh fish and brought it into the inn. Yuhong went and boiled the fish and portioned it into two bowls. The alchemist carried one bowl to the table and put the poison in it. Then, carrying the other bowl, he deliberately let loose a violent sneeze and spattered saliva onto the fish. The alchemist said, "This bowl is defiled; I will eat it." By midnight Yuhong's belly began to hurt. The pain dragged on until dawn. The alchemist went to a doctor for a pain-relieving medicine, but once it was decocted and swallowed, the pain grew worse. By noon Yuhong's hair was coming loose and his lips were split; the belly pain was unendurable. Suspecting that the alchemist had poisoned him, he begged him: "I have only fifty-five taels of silver. If you can save my life, I will give you half of everything." By then Yuhong could no longer get out of bed. The alchemist took his silver and put it in his own bundle, then came to the bedside, gave him a medicine, and said, "I am a man of the road; I make my living gathering other people's silver. You are a cunning one; you swindled fifty taels out of me. Now I have gained only five taels extra from you. Out of the goodness of my heart I will give you this medicine; whether you live or die is up to your fate." Then he shouldered his baggage and fled. Yuhong hurriedly had the innkeeper decoct the medicine. Someone who recognized it said, "This is an antidote for arsenic." After several doses in a row, the pain gradually eased. He then found a doctor near the inn to treat him, and after three days he finally recovered. The silver had all been taken by the alchemist, and he could only beg for food along the road as he made his way home.

Note: No one knew better than Yuhong how to guard against elixir tricks. A hundred schemes could not swindle him; on the contrary, he swindled the alchemist out of nearly all his capital. You could call him clever in the extreme. Yet in the end the man poisoned him: all the silver went back, five taels more besides, and he nearly lost his life. Lucky to survive, he had to beg his way home along the road, toil and humiliation enough. Can an alchemist's elixir refining be believed?
